coordinator_cost.verdict: The reference-patch rule is cheap and it pays for itself twice over, but not the way it was sold. Writing three throwaway solutions cost about 8.5 minutes and 12 frontier turns -- against a worker spend of $0.13 for one usable implementation, that is not obviously a saving. Its real value was diagnostic: the M-2 patch is what surfaced that L-4 supersedes three shipped fixtures, before a single worker token was spent, and the M-5 patch is what caught an anchoring rule that would have broken an assertion the shipped T-3 oracle already made. Both would otherwise have been discovered as a red gate at $0.09 a look.

findings: The class is on. M-5, M-8, M-6a and M-6b all went green on the first attempt, on one outcome, one writable file and one attainable red oracle each, for between $0.011 and $0.040 a packet.

Rule 9 held on every packet that tested it. The only packet that ever failed on the model's side, V5-M2, was the only restructuring one; every additive packet since has gone green first attempt. V5-M2's attempt 1 is still the clearest evidence: the worker emitted 131072 output tokens without producing a single tool call and was truncated before any write landed.

The reference patch did not buy correctness. Two packets frozen without one both went green first attempt and were the cheapest runs of the session. What a reference patch bought, twice, was catching a bad packet before dispatch -- and on M-6a the L-2b read trace caught exactly that class of defect for free.

Hand-pass item A is the highest-leverage line changed all session. Before it, oracle_reads_within_paths was unobtainable for every Python oracle in the repository, because openat's directory-fd argument was being resolved against the checkout. After it, three packets validated with all three of rule 2's fields true -- and on M-6a the restored check immediately rejected an over-broad oracle that would otherwise have been dispatched.

The loop still cannot finish. remote-add and push work; pr-create dies on GitHub's 65536-character body limit, and the branch it pushes points at starting_commit because the driver never commits the worker's changes. Two additive fixes in an unprotected file stand between here and an unattended PR.
M-1's gate-red-twice stop fired in production on the second packet it ever saw, on exactly the evidence it was designed to read, and refused the hand-off. The L-2 stop conditions work.

Six shipped fixtures were superseded across the session -- three by L-4, two by M-8, one helper by M-8's git calls. Each carries a comment naming what superseded it. A row that changes what an earlier row pinned is normal in a sequenced track; the discipline that made it safe was giving every supersession to a fresh author rather than editing the oracle to fit the implementation.
L-1b is done as-is: the opencode export path is removed rather than repaired, and the worker transcript survives in the run receipt's worker.stdout beside the receipt. It is no longer a debt line.

findings.summary: A packet's gate runs only that packet's oracle, so a diff can pass its gate and still break a contract the oracle never exercises. M-9's positional PR_STEP_NAMES indexing did exactly that; the §4.6 merge-preview caught it.
findings.open_question: whether a packet should carry a second, broader command as a non-starts_red guard wherever one is green at the starting commit. M-6a did exactly that and it cost nothing.

findings.summary: Rule 9 bounds additive-vs-restructuring but not how much is added. Both packets were additive and single-file, and both finished with finish_reason: length at 131072 output tokens having emitted no tool call. M-10 added four things at once.
findings.proposed: bound a mechanical_bulk packet by the number of independent additions as well as by their kind; the oracle's own class partition is a usable seam.

findings.summary: A frozen oracle was proven red at starting_commit and never proven green anywhere. It contained a fixture no correct implementation could pass, and the packet still validated fit: prepare's registered-commands-green-cold and acceptance-properties-discriminating both check redness, not attainability. The worker spent 1 509 082 tokens against a 1 000 000 ceiling chasing it.
findings.cost: $0.149579 and one wasted dispatch, plus the re-freeze
findings.why_it_got_through: rule 2 made oracle.reference_patch SHOULD at Amendment 2, and rules 9-11 tightened the packet's shape without ever requiring the oracle be shown green against a known-good implementation. Cutting an inherited oracle into three, as the M-10 split did, is exactly the operation that can introduce this and exactly the case where no reference patch existed.
findings.proposed: for any packet whose oracle was cut, inherited or otherwise not written fresh against a known-good implementation, require proof of green in both directions before dispatch. It does not need a throwaway solution: running the oracle against a rejected attempt's own diff found this in one command, and for a fresh oracle a reference patch already reports oracle_attainable.
findings.related: rule-11-narrowed-the-gate -- both are the same shape: the gate measures less than the reader assumes it does.

findings.summary: Every packet since V5-M9 carried the same limits block: soft 500000, hard 1000000. Observed spend ranges from 206 566 tokens (M-10a) to 1 509 082 (M-10c attempt 1) -- and varies by nearly 3x between runs of one unchanged packet. A single constant is inside that variance band, so it stops runs that would have succeeded, at random.
findings.note: the ceiling did its job as written; the fault is that the number was copied from packet to packet rather than set for each. Cost never came close to binding: $0.15 against $3.00.
findings.proposed: Treat a hard token stop as a soft outcome when the cost cap is untouched: let gate run on the work already produced rather than discarding it. Two of M-10c's three runs produced correct diffs that were thrown away while cost stood at $0.15 against a $3.00 cap. Setting limits per packet from fixture count does NOT solve this, because the variance is run-to-run.
findings.correction: an earlier reading of attempt 1 attributed its token burn to the oracle defect. Attempt 2 on the fixed oracle spent 1 435 896 tokens, so the oracle defect was real but was not the cause of the burn. Both facts stand independently.
findings.correction_2: Attempt 3 falsifies this finding's central claim. It stated the ceiling 'sits below what the packet costs'; attempt 3 ran the same packet for 533 033 tokens, well under the original 1000000. Spend on an unchanged packet varied 1 509 082 / 1 435 896 / 533 033 -- a factor of nearly three. The ceiling did not sit below the packet's cost; it sat inside the packet's variance band, which is a different and more awkward problem: no single constant is safe, and calibrating per packet from fixture count would not have helped either, because the variation is between runs of the SAME packet.

findings.summary: M-9's oracle pinned PR_STEP_NAMES as an exact 4-tuple and its real-git proof asserted the commit's diff equals the gate's touched paths exactly. M-10c's spec row requires inserting receipt-capture at the head and requires the captured files to be in the commit. Both assertions therefore had to fail, and templates/dispatch/tests/** is protected, so no worker could reconcile them. M-10c's own gate was green; the merge-preview was red at 7.
findings.caught_by: the §4.6 merge-preview, for the second time. It has now caught more real defects than the gates have.
findings.classification: coordinator defect at freeze time. Freezing a packet that changes a shape a prior oracle pinned must carry the prior oracle's reconciliation.
findings.proposed: when freezing a packet whose spec changes a constant, a signature or a set that an existing oracle asserts, reconcile that oracle in the freeze commit. An exact-equality assertion on a shape later packets are specified to extend is the smell; assert the invariant the row actually owns instead.
findings.attestation_note: the relaxations were authored by the same session that dispatched M-10c, which is the one part of this packet with no independent attestation. Rule 4 names oracle design an owner touchpoint; PR #73 is deliberately left unmerged for that reason.

findings.summary: Twice on this branch a fix was asserted without exercising the path it guarded, and twice re-running the exploit contradicted the assertion. Once by the coordinator (a merge-preview measured before the fix was clobbered, then reported as green) and once by the reviewer (a tightened real-git check whose fixture cannot reach the withholding branch).
findings.proposed: a fix for a guard is not done until the defect it guards against has been re-injected and observed to fail. The suite being green after a fix proves nothing on its own -- it was green before, with the hole open.

findings.summary: Four real defects were caught by the section 4.6 merge-preview and none by the packet gates: M-9's positional sub-step naming, M-9's pinned PR_STEP_NAMES tuple, M-9's pinned commit path set, and L-1's REQ-003 pinning body_file to the receipt. Rule 11 narrows a packet's gate to that packet's own oracle, so a diff can satisfy its gate and still break a contract the oracle never exercises. Three of the four were coordinator defects at freeze time, which is what rule 13 now addresses.
findings.proposed: keep the merge-preview mandatory and treat a green gate as necessary but not sufficient; consider the non-starts_red broader guard the M-9 finding already raised.

findings.summary: Rule 10 says the reference patch is never committed AT starting_commit -- so the worker cannot find the answer in its own checkout. It has been implemented as never committed AT ALL: .git/info/exclude carries docs/evidence/packets/*.reference.patch. The result is that no reference patch for any packet in the programme is on main, so rule 12's green-in-both-directions proof is unverifiable after the fact for every packet, not just the ones that lack one.
findings.correction_to_review: The holistic review reported that M-1, M-2, M-5, M-8 and M-10b have their reference patches committed and that V5-M11 was the outlier. Checked against origin/main: NONE are tracked. V5-M11 is not an outlier; the gap is total, which makes the finding larger than reported rather than smaller.
findings.resolution: The two rules do not actually conflict -- rule 10 constrains the tree at starting_commit, not the repository forever. A reference patch committed with the merge is not at starting_commit and cannot reach the worker. V5-M10b's and V5-M11's are force-added here; the exclude line should be narrowed or dropped, and the four surviving earlier patches (M-1, M-2, M-5, M-8) committed from the coordinator's working copy before they are lost.

findings.summary: V5-M11 is the only M-series packet missing from main, and it is missing precisely BECAUSE it was the first fully-automated run. For M-10a, M-10c and M-10b the coordinator opened the PR by hand and added the packet JSON to the branch while doing so. The driver opens the PR without that step, and it does not commit the packet it was given -- so removing the hand step silently removed the evidence the hand step was also carrying.
findings.proposed: the receipt-capture step should commit the packet JSON alongside receipt.json and worker-stdout.txt. It is the same directory, the same commit, and the packet is already on disk in the coordinator's checkout.

findings.summary: A commit modifying templates/dispatch/scripts/hybrid_dispatch.py -- a protected path, coordinator-only, the contract that bounds the worker -- reached main inside PR #74 under the title 'feat(dispatch): a bounded PR body for the driver (M-10b)'. It was authored by a concurrent agent working the same checkout, had zero test coverage, and was never reviewed by the coordinator. Planning found the same edit attempted three times across unmerged branches (630fc31, 0a9138b), one of them carrying a fixture that asserted the wholesale copy -- i.e. asserted the regression.
findings.why_nothing_caught_it: The gate asserts protected-paths-untouched over the WORKER's commit, and the worker's commit was clean. Acceptance happens over the merged PR, onto which the coordinator had stacked this commit. PR #74's gate table truthfully read protected-paths-untouched: true while that PR modified a protected path.
findings.classification: harness and process, not a tier failure. No worker was involved.
findings.remediated_by: this hand-pass: the provider copy is narrowed so no credential can travel, the containment prefix is defined once and shared with the qualification probe, the PR body now names the commit the gate covered and says later commits were not gated, and a CI check fails any PR touching a protected path unless its title declares 'hand-pass:'.

findings.summary: The justification given for --set-home -- that without it the contained worker was reading the coordinator's ~/.ssh, ~/.config/gh and opencode auth store -- does not hold. Probed directly as agentworker: those paths exist but are NOT readable; filesystem permissions already denied them. --set-home points the worker's HOME at its own rather than at one it cannot read. It is hygiene, not a boundary, and the fixtures say so.
findings.what_the_probe_did_establish: OPENCODE_CONFIG_CONTENT REPLACES rather than merges -- the worker has no opencode config or auth store anywhere and /home/agentworker does not exist -- so a provider registry must travel in the overlay or a model alias cannot resolve. And the worker completed real inference with no credential file at all, which makes options.apiKey in the overlay the ONLY credential-shaped value that ever crosses the boundary. That is what makes narrowing the copy the whole of the credential story rather than part of it.

findings.summary: The PR step pushed git push origin <branch>:<branch> with the branch fixed in worktree.branch, so a retry collided with its own earlier attempt: 'Updates were rejected because the remote contains work that you do not have locally'. Every retry reaching the PR step would hit it; none had reached it before, which is why it surfaced only after the loop started finishing end to end.
findings.fixed_by: V5-M13 (#80). A retry pushes <branch>.attempt-N and leaves the earlier branch alone.
findings.why_not_force_push: attempt 1's branch is the evidence the retry was authored against. The retry moves and the record stays -- the same shape as the owner's ruling on the attempt counter.

findings.summary: The last four rows form a chain, each found only because the previous one landed. M-10b made the loop finish end to end; finishing end to end meant the packet evidence stopped being committed, because the hand step had been carrying it. Holistic review of the finished loop found the secret scan far weaker than its fixtures suggested, which became M-12. M-12's first attempt shipped a regex that backtracked, caught only because the merge-preview ran 92 seconds instead of 30. M-12's retry then could not push at all, which became M-13. None of these were visible before the loop worked.
findings.note: This is the argument for finishing a mechanism before hardening it: four real defects were reachable only once the thing ran.

reference_patch_cost.verdict: Four reference patches cost about 9.9 minutes and 16 frontier turns. Their value was diagnostic rather than instructive: two of the four surfaced a defect before a worker token was spent (M-2's oracle supersession, M-5's over-tight anchoring rule), and none of the four was ever seen by the worker. Then the two packets frozen WITHOUT one -- the first ever -- both went green first attempt, at $0.0173 and $0.0112, the cheapest runs of the session. On additive packets the reference patch is not buying correctness. What it buys is early detection of a bad packet, and on M-6a the L-2b read trace bought that instead, for nothing. The honest reading: keep it optional, and let validate's own checks be the freeze-time gate.

OPEN, found 2026-08-25 by reading the tool's own output: a scorecard generated DURING the session it measures reports frontier sessions 0, turns 0 and usage_equivalent_usd 0.0, because the Stop hook writes a cost row per turn and the current turn has not ended. Arithmetically correct, and it reads to any human as 'the coordinator cost nothing'. The worker side carries cost_reported and total_reliable to distinguish 'measured zero' from 'not measured'; the frontier side has no equivalent and needs one. Seventh instance of the section 3h pattern, and this one is in the measuring instrument.

OPEN, found 2026-08-25 on devbox; CORRECTED the same day after the owner challenged the explanation. The first version of this line said prepare's worker-writability probe is skipped on hosts with no agentworker user, 'which includes the workstation'. Both halves were wrong and neither was checked before it was written: agentworker exists on the workstation too (uid 1101, in agentdispatch), and passwordless sudo to it works there. The actual cause is an environment variable. --worker-user defaults to os.environ.get('AGENTOPS_WORKER_USER'); devbox's agent login shell exports it as agentworker and the workstation does not set it at all, so on the workstation worker_user is None and worker_can_write returns True on its first line -- 'no worker user: writes happen as the coordinator' -- without ever reaching the group check or the sudo probe. So whether the containment check runs at all depends on an unexported variable in whichever shell invokes the suite. That is worse than depending on which users exist, because it is invisible in the repo, invisible in the test output, and differs between two hosts that both have the user. RetryWorkspaceReuseTests was green here for two weeks without exercising the probe once. The read_trace half of L-2b reports 'skipped:untraced' precisely so a skipped check cannot read as a passed one; this probe reports nothing.

OPEN, found 2026-08-25: _prepare_receipt in test_hybrid_dispatch_handpass.py parses prepare's stdout as JSON and discards the exit code and stderr on the way, so a prepare that exits non-zero surfaces as JSONDecodeError: Expecting value: line 1 column 1. RESOLVED 2026-08-25 in #124. A withholding now writes a stub receipt -- numbers and stable pattern names only, never transcript text, re-scanned before it is written -- shaped so worker_totals reads it exactly as it reads a full receipt. Original entry: OPEN, found 2026-08-25 by reading the V6 scorecard against the PRs: a WITHHELD receipt is invisible to worker_totals, which reads receipts and cannot count one that was never written. V6-D's receipt was withheld on a secret-scanner false positive, so the v6 scorecard reports 2 tasks and $0.052794 for a tract that ran 3 and cost $0.094902 -- short by a third -- while reporting cost_reported true, because that flag means every contributing receipt reported its spend and a receipt that never arrived contributes nothing to contradict. cost_unreported_tasks is empty for the same reason. Fixing it means the scorecard has to know how many tasks it SHOULD have found, i.e. read the packets or the driver reports and not only the receipts.

RESOLVED 2026-08-25 in #124. The recorded cause was a guess and was wrong: it is not that a regex constant looks like an assignment, it is that the scan ran over JSON-ESCAPED transcript text, where a newline is the two characters '\' and 'n'. secret_assignment bounds its value with \S{20,}, which stops at a real newline and not at an escaped one, so the run crossed line boundaries. What actually matched, three times in one session, was WORKER_PLACEHOLDER_API_KEY = "local-only" -- an eleven-character value whose length came entirely from the escapes after it. The scan now decodes escapes first, which also FINDS secrets that '\"' previously hid. Verified against the three real withheld transcripts. Original entry: OPEN, found 2026-08-25: SECRET_PATTERNS['secret_assignment'] matches any identifier ending in token/secret/password/api_key bound to a 20+ character value, which a regex constant satisfies. TOKEN = re.compile(r'^[a-z0-9][a-z0-9._-]*$') in a file the worker read cost V6-D its entire receipt. Failing closed is the right default; loosening a secret scanner is a judgement call with an obvious failure mode, so this is recorded rather than done.

OPEN, observed 2026-08-25 rather than predicted: parallel freezes collide on agentops.dispatch.json. Three worker rows frozen off the same main each registered a command id in that one file, and merging all three conflicted; resolved by taking the union of the command maps. The L-6 D-9 design named this as a blocker for fan-out -- eight parallel freezes cannot each register into one protected file -- and three packets were enough to demonstrate it.
